column3: This is VLA Forge. You describe a task in plain words, and it trains a robot policy for it. All of this runs in simulation.
The canvas starts blank. I type one task for an SO-101: put the blue block in the front-left slot of the tray.
The agents write the success check, collect demos, fine-tune from the closest skill, then test the policy on {n} scenes it never saw. The waiting is sped up four times, and the badge shows it.
The first round got {r1} of {rn}, under the bar, so the critic sent it back for another.
The new skill trained in {t} seconds and got {s} of {n} held-out scenes, in simulation.
Now I type add another SO-101, and a second arm appears in place.
Then I describe a task for two arms: one seats the housing in the pallet, and the other inserts it into the socket.
The Arms list gives plain results: {ac} of {an} tries finished by both arms, in simulation.
Next, the Optimize step. This is a saved run on socket insertion, scored on the same one hundred scenes every round.

Each tile is one scene, blue for a success and red for a failure. Llama 4 Maverick reads where the skill fails and proposes one change per round. A change is kept only if success rises on the same scenes.
Round zero got {o0} of one hundred. The best round, round three, got {ob}. Rounds four and five were reverted.
Here is one scene before and after. The intervals overlap, so call this an improvement in this run, not proof. All of it in simulation.
That is VLA Forge: describe a task, add arms, and measure the result, in simulation.
